clue.text: Serious single chap, but not first rate

indicators.note: first rate is A1, so 'not first rate' tells you to drop the grade letter from the chap

parts.note: sole means one and only
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A grave bachelor who is, sadly, rather second-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first rate, so the A is the letter lost from MAN, leaving SOLE + MN = SOLEMN.
explanation.definitionFit: Solemn and serious are close synonyms describing a grave, unsmiling manner.

clue.text: Prudish indignation about noisy disturbance

indicators.note: the answer is lying about in, that is scattered within, the run of words before it

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A prim person bristles with indignation at the racket of a rowdy party.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two words: prudiSH INDIGnation.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is a lively, noisy party or a commotion, so it can mean a noisy disturbance.

clue.text: I got rid of female insect

indicators.note: getting rid of something means removing it, so the named letter comes out of the name

parts.note: a female first name
taken as written: the letter to remove

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of having ditched a woman who was a pest.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I out of the girl's name LOUISE to leave LOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A louse is a small wingless parasitic insect living on the skin or hair of animals.

clue.text: Religious sage's head wear is guarded by scholars

indicators.note: something guarded is surrounded by its guards, so the headgear sits inside the scholars

parts.note: two MAs, Masters of Arts
a hat is worn on the head

explanation.surface: A holy man's headdress is protected by learned attendants.
explanation.walkthrough: MA (Master of Arts) twice, plural for scholars, with HAT inside: MA-HAT-MA. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma, meaning great soul, is a title given in India to a revered holy person, most famously Gandhi.

clue.text: Is naughty, having drink after work

indicators.note: after sets the order: the drink is written second, behind the word for work

parts.note: to act is to function or work
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Someone misbehaves after downing a drink at the end of the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the drink first, but 'after' sends it to the back. Sup is an old-fashioned word for sipping a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is to behave badly, which is what a naughty child does.

clue.text: Olympian Lord John upset a contemporary

parts.note: Sebastian, Lord Coe, Olympic champion runner

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so this word reads bottom to top

parts.note: john is slang for a toilet, as is lav

explanation.surface: A titled Olympic athlete annoys a peer named John.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a person but is slang for a lavatory. COE + LAV reversed gives COEVAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A coeval is a person of the same age or period, i.e. a contemporary.

clue.text: Point to the US as model

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the preceding letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone holds up America as an example to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like a verb meaning indicate, but it is the noun: a point of the compass.
explanation.definitionFit: South-east is one of the compass points, halfway between south and east.

clue.text: A fine sentence?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a punishment handed down by a court

explanation.surface: It reads like praise for a well-turned sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine sentence' suggests elegant writing; both words are really punishments.
explanation.definitionFit: A penalty is any punishment for breaking a rule, which covers both a fine and a judicial sentence.

clue.text: Lobbyists and journalists rue getting mixed up with the Mob

parts.note: the press is journalists collectively

indicators.note: mixed up means jumbled, so the letters of the short word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a mob is a crowd or group

explanation.surface: Reporters regret being drawn into organised crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Mob' suggests the Mafia, but here it is just a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressure group campaigns to influence government policy, which is exactly what lobbyists do.

clue.text: Tell untruth to get university place

parts.note: to lie is to tell an untruth
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An applicant fibs to secure a university place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'University place' reads as an admission, but place is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieu is French for place, used in English in the phrase 'in lieu of', meaning in place of.

clue.text: Rugby players are funny chaps!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., a London rugby union club
second meaning: clowns of traditional pantomime and commedia dell'arte

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that rugby players are a comic bunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlequins is a famous London rugby club, and a harlequin is a masked, motley-clad stage clown.

clue.text: Dave recreated Right for commercial

indicators.note: something recreated is made anew, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Dave remade a right-wing television ad.
explanation.definitionFit: An advert is an advertisement, and a television commercial is one kind of advertisement.

clue.text: Female student captivated by seal, which is found on the beach

definitions.text: which is found on the beach

indicators.note: someone captivated is held captive, so these letters are held inside the animal's name

parts.note: taken as written
she is the female pronoun
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A young woman studying marine life falls for a seal on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: L for learner is the usual crossword student. The definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Seashells wash up on beaches, so a thing found on the beach is a fair, if loose, description.

clue.text: Uninformed chap can be uncouth or amusing

indicators.note: uncouth means rough and unpolished, suggesting the following letters are in disorder

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An ill-informed man may be boorish or entertaining.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant person, someone lacking knowledge, so an uninformed chap.

clue.text: Oscar mutters sadly about love on the very margins

parts.note: O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters go round the zero
sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of the verb are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: Oscar grumbles unhappily about love, feeling left on the fringes.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters wrap around the zero for love, all placed after the opening Oscar; love as zero comes from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Outermost means furthest from the centre, which is to be on the extreme edge.

clue.text: German woman getting high

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German
a woman's first name

explanation.surface: A German woman gets intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' suggests drugs; here it describes meat or game that has been hung until strong-smelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamy (or gamey) meat has the strong flavour of game that has been hung, which is the culinary sense of high.

clue.text: China tea

definitions.meaning: first meaning: friend, from Cockney rhyming slang china plate = the answer
second meaning: a South American herbal tea, also spelt maté

explanation.walkthrough: 'China tea' looks like a single drink from China; China here is rhyming slang.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney slang a china is a pal, a friend; separately, maté is a caffeine-rich infusion drunk in South America.

clue.text: Rich financial journalist?

parts.note: money is the subject of finance
ED is short for editor

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, 'financial journalist' is a money editor, a MONEY ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Moneyed means having plenty of money, that is, wealthy.

clue.text: "Goodness!" I uttered nervously, having ingested cocaine

indicators.note: ingested means swallowed, so the drug goes inside the rest
said nervously, the words come out jittery and disordered, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken letter for letter
C is slang for cocaine

explanation.surface: Someone high on cocaine exclaims 'Goodness!' in a jittery voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goodness!' looks like an exclamation, but it is the noun meaning virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectitude is moral uprightness, the quality of being good and righteous.

clue.text: Part-exchange vehicle, accepting Ecstasy and diamonds in return

indicators.note: something accepting another thing takes it in, so the vehicle holds the pair

parts.note: a train is a vehicle

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the two letters are written in the opposite order

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A car swapped in a deal that brought drugs and jewels back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In return' sounds like payment, but it reverses E and D before they go into TRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in is an item handed over as partial payment for a new one, i.e. a part-exchange.

clue.text: Mafia leader, a yob of yesteryear, made a charitable gesture

parts.note: a don is the head of a Mafia family
taken as written
a Teddy boy, a 1950s British youth tearaway

explanation.surface: A crime boss, once a young thug, made a philanthropic gift.
explanation.walkthrough: A ted is a Teddy boy, a member of a 1950s British youth cult known for Edwardian-style dress and rowdiness.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give to charity, so donated means made a charitable gift.

clue.text: Stick little 11 in this place

parts.note: 11-across is ADVERT, and an ad is a short advert
here means in this place

explanation.surface: Instructions to put a small advert up right here.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to stick fast to a surface, as glue or a label does.

clue.text: Starts to interrogate comparatively simple burglar

indicators.note: starts, in the plural, means the opening letters of the next word are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of the word
rude can mean primitive or simple, and ruder is its comparative

explanation.surface: Police begin questioning a rather dim housebreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Starts' takes more than one letter: the first three of interrogate, INT, then RUDER.
explanation.definitionFit: An intruder is someone who enters a place unlawfully, which is what a burglar does.

clue.text: Salmon dish contains kind of nut

indicators.note: the phrase before it holds the answer within its letters

parts.note: runs from the second letter of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A fish recipe that includes nuts, perhaps a trout-amandine style dish.
explanation.walkthrough: sALMON Dish holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The almond is the edible kernel of the almond tree, commonly called a nut.

clue.text: Clout small child, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the word is matched by its sound not spelling

parts.note: a mite is a tiny child

explanation.surface: It sounds like an order to smack a little kid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clout' looks like a verb, to hit, but it is the noun meaning power.
explanation.definitionFit: Clout as a noun means power or influence, and might is strength or power.

clue.text: Chop suey with a small portion of pickle on the side

indicators.note: chopping cuts things up, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a small portion of a word is just its first letter here

parts.note: its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Chinese takeaway order with a little pickle as a side dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chop suey' looks like one dish; chop is the anagram signal. 'On the side' looks like a serving note, but only 'side' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.

clue.text: George consumed port

parts.note: G is an abbreviation for George
ate means consumed food

explanation.surface: George drank the port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the wine George drank; it is a gateway.
explanation.definitionFit: Port in the old sense of an entrance or gateway, from Latin porta, so a gate.

clue.text: In short, Dorothy and Edward scattered!

parts.note: Dot is a pet form of Dorothy
Ted is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: Dorothy and Edward fled in all directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' tells you to use the shortened forms of both names.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotted can mean spread here and there, as in houses dotted about a hillside.

clue.text: One half of the country

definitions.meaning: first meaning: joined together as one
second meaning: one of the two words in ... Kingdom or ... States

explanation.surface: A remark about a divided nation.
explanation.definitionFit: United means joined into a single whole, and it is one word of the two-word name United Kingdom.
